::: {#rem-scaling}

#### What the scaling prevents

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
d_k, n_keys = 512, 64
q_draws = torch.randn(1_000, 1, d_k, generator=generator)
k_draws = torch.randn(1_000, n_keys, d_k, generator=generator)
raw_scores = (q_draws @ k_draws.transpose(1, 2)).squeeze(1)
top_raw = torch.softmax(raw_scores, dim=1).max(dim=1).values.mean().item()
top_scaled = torch.softmax(raw_scores / math.sqrt(d_k), dim=1).max(dim=1).values.mean().item()
print(top_raw, top_scaled)
```

With $d_k = `r py$d_k`$ and `r py$n_keys` keys drawn as in @exr-dot-variance,
the unscaled [softmax](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/multiclass-logistic-regression.html#def-softmax) gives its largest weight an average of `r sprintf("%.2f", py$top_raw)`,
so each query mostly copies one value.
After dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$,
the largest weight averages `r sprintf("%.2f", py$top_scaled)`.
@vaswani2017attention [section 3.2.1] suggest why the scaling helps:
where one weight is near 1,
the softmax's [gradient](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/linear-regression.html#def-gradient) is near 0,
and training slows.

:::
